title: Reward Hacking the Classroom
author: Becky Allen
summary: Allen asks what happens if assessment is treated as the reward function for an AI system that optimises teaching, drawing on a podcast discussion of the difficulties of reinforcement learning with sparse, delayed feedback. She identifies three traps: short-run success that damages long-run learning, the collapse of multidimensional understanding into one score, and the fact that weighting goals is a value judgment rather than a technical choice. She also notes that an optimiser may seek the roughly fifty percent success rate that gives it the most information, which conflicts with mastery teaching. Human teachers, she says, work like model-based predictors who read surprise cues in real time, and multimodal tutors may imitate this, but that only moves the verification problem deeper. Her conclusion is that education is a Diet problem, not a Sudoku problem, so AI tutors risk chasing scores over educated minds.
points: Treating exam scores as a reward function invites the same overfitting that plagues AI benchmarks.
A single mark hides the multiple dimensions of understanding a teacher cares about, so shallow and deep strategies look identical to the optimiser.
Weighting joy, retention and test performance is an ethical choice, and an optimiser will exploit whichever is prioritised.
An RL tutor has a perverse incentive to push students toward failure, because that produces more information than mastery does.
Gaze-tracking tutors solve data sparsity but risk training compliance, because someone must still decide which outcomes count as good.
quotes: RL has a powerful incentive to steer students into regimes where they can reliably pass this test: narrow the curriculum, polish exam technique, postpone the awkward, generative work that is harder to score. “Teaching to the test” is simply the educational version of an RL agent overfitting to a narrow eval. You can ratchet up performance on a specific specification of “success” while leaving the underlying competence brittle and narrow.

Verification is the heart of the problem. If a shallow pattern-match and a deep, general strategy both earn full marks, the reward function cannot distinguish between them. To the optimiser, they are equivalent trajectories through state space. In the classroom, those two paths look utterly different to a teacher watching the work unfold. On the mark scheme, they are identical.

In practice, the optimiser ruthlessly exploits whatever you prioritise. If the reward function weights “engagement” (as in many language apps), the system will produce highly addictive experiences with thin educational value. If it weights “current exam performance,” it will produce rote drilling. Just as AI models effectively “game” their benchmarks, an RL tutor will pursue the specific definition of success we give it with more determination than wisdom, trampling over every unmeasured value in the process.

In short, the system could be incentivised to sacrifice the student’s learning (which needs stability) to maximise its own verification speed (which needs variance). We risk building tutors that are very efficient at “learning the student,” but quite poor at teaching them.

But while this solves the data problem, it exacerbates the alignment problem. A human teacher perceives that a student staring out the window might be deeply processing a complex idea. An RL system optimising for “engagement metrics” sees only a loss of focus. If we treat “eyes on screen” as a proxy for “learning in brain,” we risk building effective optimisers of compliance, training students to perform the “stare of the dead” to satisfy the algorithm, rather than optimisers of thought.

Teachers, however, operate much more like Model-Based RL or Active Inference agents. They do not wait for the exam result to update their strategy. Instead, they maintain a rich, internal generative model of the classroom—a simulation of how students think—and they optimise against that in real time.

Ultimately, the verification problem remains unsolved. We are attempting to build machines that optimise for “learning,” yet we lack a ground-truth function to check if they have succeeded without resorting to the very tests that distort the process. Until we can verify deep understanding as cleanly as we verify a checkmate, reinforcement learning will remain the wrong hammer for this nail. We can build agents that chase leaderboards, but we should not mistake high scores for educated minds.
